questions.q: State the two essential properties of the material used for the filament of an incandescent bulb and explain why each property is necessary.
questions.a: The filament material (tungsten) must have: (1) High resistivity — so that a short length of thin wire offers high resistance, producing sufficient heat (H = I²Rt) at 220 V. (2) High melting point (≈ 3380 °C) — so that the filament can glow at 2500–3000 °C without melting. A wrong answer (e.g., "low resistance to allow more current") reveals confusion between connecting wires (which should have low resistance) and heating elements (which need high resistance).

questions.q: Why is the fuse wire always connected in series with the live wire of the circuit, and why must it have a low melting point but the connecting wires must have high melting points?
questions.a: Fuse is in series so that the same current flows through it and the appliance; if current exceeds the safe limit, the fuse melts first, breaking the circuit and stopping current to the appliance. Fuse wire has low melting point (e.g., tin-lead alloy ≈ 200 °C) to melt quickly under overload. Connecting wires have high melting point (copper ≈ 1085 °C) so they don't melt during normal operation or brief overloads. A wrong answer (e.g., "fuse in parallel") shows misunderstanding of series current and the protective role of a fuse.

questions.q: An electric heater rated 1500 W, 220 V is connected to a 220 V supply. Calculate: (a) the current drawn, (b) the resistance of the heating element, and (c) the heat energy produced in 10 minutes. (Use H = I²Rt or H = Pt)
questions.a:
Given: P = 1500 W, V = 220 V, t = 10 min = 600 s.
Step 1: Current I = P/V = 1500/220 = 6.818 A (≈ 6.82 A).
Step 2: Resistance R = V/I = 220/6.818 = 32.26 Ω (or R = V²/P = 220²/1500 = 32.27 Ω).
Step 3: Heat energy H = P × t = 1500 × 600 = 9,00,000 J = 9 × 10⁵ J.
(Alternatively H = I²Rt = (6.818)² × 32.27 × 600 ≈ 9 × 10⁵ J).
A wrong answer using H = V²t/R without converting time to seconds reveals unit inconsistency; using P = VI but forgetting to convert minutes to seconds gives H = 1500 × 10 = 15000 J (wrong).

questions.q: Two bulbs are marked 60 W, 220 V and 100 W, 220 V. Which bulb has higher resistance? If they are connected in series across 220 V, which bulb will glow brighter? Explain using the heating effect formula.
questions.a:
Resistance R = V²/P. For 60 W: R₁ = 220²/60 = 806.7 Ω. For 100 W: R₂ = 220²/100 = 484 Ω. So the 60 W bulb has higher resistance.
In series, same current I flows through both. Heat produced per second (power dissipated) = I²R. Since R₁ > R₂, the 60 W bulb dissipates more power (I²R₁ > I²R₂) and glows brighter.
A wrong answer ("100 W bulb is brighter because it has higher wattage") ignores that wattage ratings are for parallel connection at rated voltage; in series, the higher resistance bulb gets more voltage share and more heat.

questions.q: A student replaces a blown 5 A fuse in a household circuit with a thick copper wire from a discarded cable. The circuit carries a 10 A load. Evaluate whether this is safe. What will happen to the copper wire and the connected appliances?
questions.a: Unsafe. Copper wire has very high melting point (1085 °C) and low resistivity. At 10 A (double the 5 A rating), the copper wire will NOT melt quickly; instead, it will allow the excessive current to continue flowing, overheating the appliance wiring, possibly causing fire or permanent damage. The fuse's purpose — to melt and break the circuit at a specific current — is defeated. A wrong answer ("copper wire will melt because current is high") shows ignorance of copper's high melting point and low resistivity compared to fuse alloy.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a 9 V battery, nichrome wire of different lengths, and a small LED to demonstrate that a fuse wire must be thin and of appropriate material. List the steps, observations, and conclusion.
questions.a:
Steps: (1) Connect a 30 cm nichrome wire in series with LED and 9 V battery — LED glows dimly (wire resistance limits current). (2) Replace with 5 cm nichrome wire — LED glows brighter (lower resistance, more current). (3) Replace with a thick copper wire of same length — LED glows very bright (very low resistance, high current). (4) Now short the battery with a very thin strand of steel wool (simulating fuse) — it melts instantly.
Observation: Thin, high-resistivity wire heats up and melts at lower current than thick copper wire.
Conclusion: Fuse wire must be thin (high resistance per unit length) and made of low-melting-point alloy so it melts at the rated current. A poor answer (using only copper wires of different thicknesses) fails to show the material dependence (resistivity and melting point) which is crucial for fuse design.
